#9730. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9729. International Men’s Day: Anthropic IPOs, Trump Meets Putin and Xi, and GTA 6 Is Released

Amplifying words and ideas to separate the ordinary from the extraordinary, making the mundane majestic.

Amplifying words and ideas to separate the ordinary from the extraordinary, making the mundane majestic.

Amplifying words and ideas to separate the ordinary from the extraordinary, making the mundane majestic.

November 19, 2026. Three of the world’s most powerful men meet to discuss nuclear weapons. An artificial intelligence company raises more money in a single IPO than most countries spend on technology. And millions of men finally get to steal fictional cars in Vice City.

An ⁠excellent Venn diagram circulating on X captured the extraordinary coincidence of three events occurring on November 19, 2026.

Someone in our HackerNoon Slack channel pointed out the final coincidence: it’s International Men’s Day.

The joke is funny enough on its own. But the more you investigate the actual news, the stranger the connections become.

Elon Musk thinks AI might eventually generate games like GTA without traditional developers. Anthropic’s CEO believes advanced AI chips should be kept away from China. Trump thinks whoever wins the race to superintelligence wins everything. Meanwhile, the leaders of the world’s largest nuclear powers are discussing how not to destroy civilization.

And Rockstar Games has just released a video game about committing crimes.

Let’s examine this particularly remarkable day in the history of men.

On November 18, Anthropic announced that it had ⁠priced its initial public offering at $83 per share.

The offering comprised 980 million shares, representing approximately $81.34 billion in gross proceeds before expenses and excluding any additional shares sold through the underwriters’ option.

Not all of that money goes to Anthropic. Approximately 23.6 million shares were being sold by existing stockholders.

Nevertheless, it was an extraordinary amount of money.

When Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on November 19, shares opened at $111.50.

That’s approximately 34% above the IPO price.

As ⁠Barron’s reported when trading began, investors who received shares at the offering price immediately found themselves holding something worth considerably more.

The $83 price also happens to be almost identical to the price of GTA VI.

For approximately $80, Rockstar gives you a fictional world where you can do almost anything.

For $83, Anthropic gives eligible IPO investors a tiny ownership stake in a company trying to build artificial intelligence that might eventually do almost anything.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has spent years arguing that increasingly powerful artificial intelligence could fundamentally transform society.

Now public investors get to bet on that argument.

In an ⁠interview following the IPO, Amodei reflected on how rapidly the technology’s economic implications had become real:

“I don’t think we really believed it until it actually happened.”

His sister, Anthropic cofounder and president Daniela Amodei, characterized the IPO as another milestone rather than the destination:

“it’s like one stop on the journey, right?”

The company has also warned investors that its commitments to AI safety may sometimes conflict with maximizing profits.

What happens when shareholders want Anthropic to make more money, but Anthropic’s leadership believes making more money would create unacceptable risks?

Senator Elizabeth Warren has already raised concerns about exposing investors and retirement savings to the risks surrounding advanced AI.

In a statement ahead of the offering, she argued:

“The SEC must protect investors and Congress must act quickly to put in place safeguards on advanced AI development.”

The broader contradiction is difficult to ignore.

Anthropic was founded partly because its creators believed advanced AI required extraordinary caution.

Now it is participating in one of the largest financial spectacles in stock-market history.

Apparently, protecting humanity is extremely capital-intensive.

While Anthropic was making financial history in New York, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin were making diplomatic history in Shenzhen, China.

The three leaders held an unprecedented trilateral summit on November 19 during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering.

According to ⁠Reuters’ account of the meeting, nuclear weapons and the war in Ukraine were among the major subjects.

Xi described the gathering as a historic opportunity for cooperation.

Putin emphasized that the three countries shared interests in resolving regional conflicts, including Ukraine.

There is something extraordinary about three men collectively representing such enormous military and economic power sitting around a table to discuss whether they can trust one another.

Especially when you read what they actually said.

During the summit, Trump offered a remarkably straightforward explanation of why nuclear disarmament is difficult.

According to the ⁠published transcript of his remarks:

“Once you have the nuclear weapons, it’s very hard to not have them.”

“It’s very hard to give them up as the leader of a country.”

They are also the sort of statements that sound like a man explaining why he still has a garage full of things he purchased fifteen years ago.

Except the garage contains nuclear warheads.

Trump also praised Shenzhen, telling the gathering:

“They have a major city, one of the biggest cities anywhere in the world, and it’s flawless.”

The president of the United States was discussing global security while also delivering what sounded like a five-star hotel review.

Before the trilateral meeting, Trump greeted Putin warmly.

According to ⁠ABC News’ coverage, Trump referred to the Russian president as:

He also praised their longstanding relationship.

That friendship is politically consequential, given Russia’s continuing war against Ukraine and the enormous disagreements between Washington and Moscow.

Trump’s remarks illustrate the central tension of the summit: personal relationships between leaders are being presented as a potential route toward resolving conflicts involving millions of people.

Whether those relationships produce meaningful agreements remains another question.

The leaders endorsed a declaration emphasizing the importance of reducing nuclear risks.

“a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought”

It is also a principle the major nuclear powers have endorsed before.

The declaration did not establish a specific schedule for eliminating nuclear weapons, end the war in Ukraine, or resolve the major strategic disagreements among the three countries.

As ⁠the Associated Press observed in its analysis of the summit, the meeting’s symbolism appeared more substantial than its immediate policy achievements.

The world’s most powerful men agreed that peace is good.

Humanity will now wait to see what they do about it.

The overlap between Anthropic’s IPO and the international summit is arguably the most important part of the meme.

Advanced artificial intelligence requires enormous computing resources.

Those resources depend heavily on sophisticated semiconductors, including Nvidia’s most advanced chips.

And access to those chips has become a central dispute between the United States and China.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has been particularly outspoken about this issue.

In his ⁠essay about DeepSeek and American export controls, Amodei argued:

“Export controls serve a vital purpose: keeping democratic nations at the forefront of AI development.”

His argument is that restricting access to advanced computing hardware can help preserve America’s technological advantage.

China, unsurprisingly, sees restrictions on access to advanced technology rather differently.

During his visit to China, Trump discussed the competition to develop superintelligence.

His summary was characteristically direct:

SI refers to superintelligence: artificial intelligence that exceeds human capabilities across a broad range of intellectual tasks.

Trump’s statement captures the geopolitical stakes in six words.

The economy? Military superiority? Scientific progress? Control over the future?

At APEC, Trump also rejected international restrictions that could constrain American AI development.

As ⁠ABC News reported, Trump opposed what he called globalist regulation of advanced AI.

Meanwhile, Xi emphasized international cooperation and human oversight.

The Chinese government’s account of his position called for countries to:

“ensure that AI is always under human control”

These competing positions reveal a remarkable situation.

The United States wants to maintain its lead in artificial intelligence.

China wants greater access to advanced computing and a meaningful role in setting global rules.

Anthropic wants to develop increasingly capable AI while maintaining its safety commitments.

And investors want all of these companies to make money.

These objectives are not necessarily compatible.

Yet they are increasingly shaping the same global economy.

While world leaders were discussing nuclear weapons and investors were buying shares in Anthropic, Rockstar Games finally released Grand Theft Auto VI.

The company confirmed the launch in its ⁠official November 19 announcement.

The game is available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.

Its standard edition costs $79.99 in the United States.

That is $3.01 less than Anthropic’s IPO price.

Unlike an Anthropic share, however, the game comes with an entire fictional criminal economy.

Players return to Vice City and the fictional state of Leonida, following the story of Jason and Lucia.

It has been more than thirteen years since Grand Theft Auto V arrived in September 2013.

Rockstar delayed GTA VI several times before settling on November 19, 2026.

In its ⁠final major delay announcement, the company explained:

“these extra months will allow us to finish the game with the level of polish you have come to expect and deserve.”

Apparently, building a realistic simulation of American criminality takes longer than building some forms of artificial intelligence.

Rockstar’s parent company, Take-Two Interactive, is publicly traded.

Its CEO, Strauss Zelnick, has repeatedly emphasized the enormous commercial significance of GTA VI.

“a lot of people will be calling in sick on November 19”

That is a remarkable prediction from the CEO of a publicly traded company.

Imagine Anthropic’s CEO announcing that the company’s next AI model would cause millions of employees to stop showing up for work.

Actually, that’s not too far from what some people in the AI industry have been predicting.

Take-Two previously forecast approximately $8 billion to $8.2 billion in net bookings for fiscal 2027.

Those figures cover the company’s broader business, not just GTA VI.

Nevertheless, they demonstrate the scale of the expectations surrounding the launch.

The connections become even stranger when Elon Musk enters the story.

Musk has repeatedly argued that generative artificial intelligence will eventually transform video game development.

Instead of spending years and billions of dollars building a game, developers might eventually describe the world they want and let AI generate it.

In January 2026, Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch suggested:

“There’s definitely a non-zero chance we get ‘generate your own GTA 6 in a few minutes’ before GTA 6.”

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney also entertained the possibility of AI-generated games.

The broader discussion concerned whether systems capable of generating images, video, and software could eventually generate entire interactive worlds.

That possibility would fundamentally change the economics of the video game industry.

Rockstar has spent more than a decade building GTA VI.

An AI system that could generate comparable experiences in minutes would represent an extraordinary technological achievement.

But generating a playable environment is not the same as creating a coherent, polished game with compelling characters, sophisticated systems, and a consistent artistic vision.

GTA VI is a particularly useful test case because its value depends on more than the number of buildings, vehicles, or characters an AI could generate.

It depends on how all those pieces work together.

Zelnick has also challenged sweeping claims about artificial intelligence replacing human workers.

Responding to Musk’s predictions about automation, Zelnick reportedly asked:

“If AI was going to take anyone’s job, wouldn’t it take his job?”

“Maybe Elon Musk is indeed a simulation, it’s possible.”

The exchange illustrates a disagreement that extends well beyond video games.

Musk believes increasingly capable AI could dramatically reduce the need for human labor.

Zelnick runs a company whose most important product depends on thousands of people coordinating their creative and technical work over many years.

Both men have enormous financial interests in their respective visions of the future.

And both are discussing a technology that could transform the businesses they operate.

On International Men’s Day, the argument is particularly appropriate.

One billionaire thinks AI might eventually generate the work of another billionaire’s employees.

The other billionaire wonders why the first billionaire still needs to work.

There is a deeper connection between Anthropic and GTA VI.

Both companies are building systems that simulate aspects of the world.

Rockstar builds a fictional environment with characters, vehicles, economies, police departments, and social systems.

Anthropic develops AI systems designed to understand and interact with the real world through language, software, and other tools.

GTA VI’s characters exist inside a fictional world.

Claude’s outputs can influence decisions outside the computer.

But both businesses depend on the ability to represent increasingly complex aspects of human behavior.

The comparison becomes more interesting when considering the economics.

Rockstar spends years developing a world that millions of people will pay to enter.

Anthropic spends billions developing intelligence that businesses hope will make work more efficient.

Rockstar wants people to spend more time inside its product.

Anthropic’s customers often want to spend less time completing tasks.

The other sells a tool for changing reality.

And on November 19, 2026, both are asking consumers and investors to pay approximately $80 for a piece of the future.

The final overlap in the Venn diagram reads:

It is attached to GTA VI and the Trump–Xi–Putin summit.

Grand Theft Auto is a video game built around criminal activity, reckless driving, violence, and increasingly elaborate ways to behave badly.

International diplomacy, meanwhile, involves leaders making decisions with consequences for millions or billions of people.

The difference is that GTA VI has a reset button.

There is also a revealing contrast in how the two events are evaluated.

Rockstar’s success will be measured through sales, reviews, player engagement, and the quality of its game.

The summit’s success will be measured through changes in international relations, nuclear risks, military conflicts, and economic cooperation.

Rockstar can release a patch when something goes wrong.

Perhaps the most absurd part of the day is that the fictional criminal world might offer a more predictable set of rules than the real geopolitical one.

The observance was established to recognize positive male role models, celebrate men’s contributions to families and communities, and raise awareness of issues affecting men’s health and well-being.

Its stated objectives include recognizing:

“everyday, working-class men who are living decent, honest lives.”

Those men are largely absent from the Venn diagram.

There are no circles for fathers taking their children to school.

No circles for men caring for aging parents.

No circles for teachers, nurses, construction workers, or friends helping one another through difficult times.

Instead, the world’s attention is focused on billionaires, presidents, nuclear weapons, artificial intelligence, and a video game about stealing cars.

There is something appropriate about that.

International Men’s Day is partly about recognizing the positive things men contribute to society.

The day’s biggest headlines offer an unusually vivid illustration of how much power men still exercise over its future.

Some of that power produces extraordinary technological achievements.

Some produces entertainment enjoyed by millions.

And some creates risks that everyone else must live with.

The International Men’s Day organizers have emphasized that improving men’s lives benefits society more broadly.

That is a more useful principle than treating masculinity as a competition to accumulate the most money, military power, or technological influence.

There are also important women in these stories.

Anthropic cofounder Daniela Amodei helped lead the company to its public-market debut.

GTA VI features Lucia Caminos as one of its two protagonists.

And the consequences of decisions made by the three presidents in Shenzhen will affect women and men alike.

The Venn diagram is funny because it compresses three enormous stories into one ridiculous coincidence.

But the stories are connected by something more consequential than their shared date.

They are all about who gets to control the future.

Anthropic wants to build increasingly powerful artificial intelligence.

Trump, Xi, and Putin want to shape the international rules under which that technology develops.

Rockstar wants to create a fictional world so compelling that millions of people will voluntarily disappear into it.

And ordinary people are left trying to figure out what all of this means for their lives.

And if he doesn’t answer, don’t rule out Vice City.

#9727. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

#9726. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9725. Incus Project and Migration Trust Boundaries Need Separate Review

Incus gives teams a convenient way to operate containers and virtual machines, but project isolation is a security claim about who can create, inherit, and move resources. Two issues fixed in Incus 7.6.0 challenge that claim.

CVE-2026-130784 is an authorization bypass that lets restricted clients create and access default-project resources by exploiting entitlement checks against the requested project. The advisory describes two consequences: bridge networks with raw.dnsmasq directives can execute code as root on the host, and inherited resources can be manipulated through the ?project= parameter.

The lesson is that a project identifier used in an API call must be part of the authorization decision. Checking the caller against one project and acting on another is a confused-deputy pattern.

CVE-2026-130780 is a path traversal in migration handling. A malicious migration peer can supply unvalidated dependent volume and snapshot names and write outside the intended directory. The advisory notes that this can create root-owned volumes with attacker content at arbitrary host paths and can bypass storage-pool restrictions.

Migration is often considered an internal operation. Treat a migration peer as a trust-bearing principal, especially when the source is managed by another team.

Upgrade to 7.6.0 or later and verify the running daemon version. Audit restricted projects, default-project networks, inherited profiles, and any use of raw.dnsmasq. Review project-scoped API logs for mismatched project identifiers.

Inventory migration relationships and storage pools. Check for unexpected root-owned volumes, unusual directory names, and failed migration attempts near the disclosure date. If an untrusted migration source existed, preserve the daemon and host filesystem evidence before cleanup.

Deny raw configuration fields to non-administrative projects. Require explicit approval for migration peers and restrict their network reachability. Alert when a project-scoped request accesses a default or inherited resource. Test isolation with both positive and negative cases, not only with successful project creation.

#9724. This Breakfast Addition Sharpens Memory Later In The Day

A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.

A generous handful produced small cognitive benefits over the following six hours, although memory performance varied with the timing of the tests.

Walnuts may influence how the brain directs attention and obtains the energy needed for demanding mental work.

Professor Claire Williams, study co-author, said:

“A handful of walnuts with breakfast could give young adults a mental edge when they need to perform at the top of their game.”

The research involved over 30 healthy young adults aged 18–30, who ate two different breakfasts on separate visits to the laboratory.

One contained 50 g of crushed walnuts mixed into muesli and vanilla yoghurt, while the other contained no nuts.

The breakfasts contained almost identical calorie and fat totals, with butter added to the comparison meal to help achieve this match.

Participants completed tests before breakfast and again two, four and six hours afterwards, while researchers also recorded their brain activity.

After the walnut breakfast, participants responded faster on tasks involving attention, resisting distractions and switching between different mental rules.

These abilities form part of executive function, which helps us control our responses and adapt to changing demands.

The differences were modest, averaging around eight milliseconds on the attention test and 22 milliseconds when switching between rules.

Whether improvements of this size would make a noticeable difference outside the laboratory remains uncertain.

The memory findings were more complicated.

Two hours after eating walnuts, participants performed slightly worse when repeatedly learning and recalling a list of words.

By six hours, however, the pattern had reversed, with better performance after walnuts than after the comparison breakfast.

One possibility is that walnuts helped protect learning performance as the testing day wore on.

Repeated mental effort can make it harder to take in new information, so preserving the ability to learn could be useful even without improving every aspect of memory.

However, participants did not report feeling less mentally fatigued after walnuts, leaving this explanation unconfirmed.

Another possibility is that some benefits emerged gradually as nutrients were absorbed and processed.

Walnuts contain omega-3 fats, protein and plant compounds called polyphenols, which could contribute individually or together.

Electrical recordings revealed differences in frontal and parietal brain activity after the two breakfasts.

These regions contribute to attention, memory and the control of behaviour.

The changes may indicate that walnuts altered how mental resources were allocated during the tests, although they do not establish precisely why performance improved.

Blood samples also showed slightly higher glucose availability and lower concentrations of circulating free fatty acids after walnuts.

Greater glucose availability might help fuel demanding mental work.

The study was published in the journal Food & Function (Bell et al., 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9723. Next.js `revalidatePath` vs `revalidateTag` in 2026: Choosing the Right Cache Invalidation Primitive at Scale

Posted on Nov 20 • Originally published at jsmanifest.com

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Most Next.js developers reach for revalidatePath when a mutation happens. It is familiar, straightforward, and works immediately in development. The function invalidates everything under a path, ensuring users see fresh data after an update. This approach breaks down in production when applications scale beyond a single container or when cache entries multiply across dozens of routes.

The problem manifests when a product price changes. The developer calls revalidatePath('/products'), expecting the product list to refresh. The homepage also displays featured products, so they add revalidatePath('/'). The search page shows products too, so another call goes in. Within weeks, every mutation triggers a cascade of path invalidations, wiping caches that have nothing to do with the actual change.

Problem diagram showing revalidatePath invalidating unrelated cached data

Teams discover months later that a user profile update invalidates the product catalog because both routes sit under the same path prefix. Cache hit rates drop. Response times climb. Developers start questioning whether caching provides any benefit at all.

The solution requires understanding that Next.js offers two distinct primitives with fundamentally different invalidation semantics. revalidateTag targets specific cache entries by tag, leaving unrelated data intact. revalidatePath wipes everything under a URL path, regardless of whether the underlying data changed.

Solution diagram showing revalidateTag surgically invalidating only tagged data

This distinction determines whether a caching strategy scales or collapses under real traffic. The choice between these primitives shapes cache efficiency, deployment complexity, and the ability to reason about invalidation across a growing application.

revalidatePath invalidates every cache entry associated with a URL path. When a Server Action or Route Handler calls revalidatePath('/products'), Next.js marks all cached data for that route as stale. The next request triggers fresh data fetches for the entire page, regardless of which specific piece of data changed.

This primitive exists for scenarios where precise tagging is impractical or impossible. A content management system might store dozens of content types across a single route. A dashboard might aggregate data from fifteen different sources. Tracking which tags to invalidate for each mutation becomes error-prone when the page composition changes frequently.

The function accepts a second parameter controlling the scope. Setting it to 'page' invalidates only the exact path. Setting it to 'layout' invalidates the path and all nested routes. The default behavior matches 'page' in Next.js 15.3 as documented in the official revalidation guide.

Diagram showing revalidatePath invalidation scope through route hierarchy

The primitive works immediately in single-container deployments where all requests hit the same process. In-memory cache entries disappear synchronously when revalidatePath executes. Developers see instant feedback during local development and staging environments running on single instances.

The limitation surfaces when multiple routes depend on the same data but sit under different paths. A product appears on the homepage, search results, category pages, and its detail page. Invalidating the product requires calling revalidatePath for every path, or accepting stale data until the next scheduled revalidation.

Teams often solve this by calling revalidatePath('/') to invalidate the entire site. This approach sacrifices all caching benefits to avoid tracking which paths need invalidation. Response times climb as every page regenerates from scratch after any mutation.

revalidateTag invalidates cache entries that explicitly opt into a tag. Functions using the use cache directive call cacheTag('tag-name') to register their cache entry with one or more tags. Later mutations call revalidateTag('tag-name') to invalidate all entries with that tag, regardless of which routes or components created them.

This primitive scales to applications where many routes share the same underlying data. A product detail component might appear on five different pages. Tagging its cache entry with product:${id} allows a single revalidateTag call to invalidate the product everywhere it appears.

The tagging happens inside the cached function, not at the call site. This decouples cache invalidation from route structure. Components consume getProduct without knowing or caring about tags. Only the data layer manages cache semantics.

The Next.js revalidation documentation recommends passing 'max' as the second argument to revalidateTag. This sets the stale-while-revalidate window to its longest duration, allowing stale content to serve while fresh data generates in the background. Users see instant responses while cache entries refresh asynchronously.

Diagram showing revalidateTag invalidating only tagged entries across routes

The tradeoff appears in infrastructure requirements. Tag-based invalidation requires a shared cache store in multi-container deployments. The default in-memory cache cannot coordinate tags across processes. Next.js 15.3 provides unstable_cache with pluggable backends, but custom cache adapters remain necessary for production distributed systems.

Tag naming conventions matter at scale. Prefixing tags by entity type prevents collisions. product:123 and category:123 represent different entities despite sharing an ID. Including version numbers in tags like api:v2:product:123 allows gradual cache migration during API changes.

The primitive also supports cache entry hierarchies. A product page might tag its cache with both product:123 and category:electronics. Invalidating category:electronics refreshes all products in that category without knowing their individual IDs. This pattern reduces coordination complexity when relationships change.

The choice between revalidatePath and revalidateTag determines cache efficiency and maintenance burden. Each primitive excels in specific scenarios while creating problems in others.

Path-based invalidation wins when routes operate independently. An admin dashboard with dedicated data for each page benefits from path invalidation. Each route fetches distinct data that never appears elsewhere. Invalidating /admin/users affects nothing else. No tagging infrastructure provides value here.

Comparison diagram showing when path invalidation works versus when tags work

Tag-based invalidation becomes essential when data appears across many routes. E-commerce applications display products on listing pages, detail pages, search results, recommendations, and cart summaries. A price change must invalidate the product everywhere. Tracking which paths contain which products quickly becomes impossible.

The difference compounds in applications with dynamic routes. A blog with /posts/[slug] might have thousands of post pages. Invalidating a single post requires either calling revalidatePath with the exact slug or invalidating the entire posts section. Tags allow revalidateTag('post:abc123') to target exactly one post regardless of its URL.

Mutation patterns influence the decision. Applications with frequent broad updates favor path invalidation. A stock market dashboard might refresh all displayed stocks every few seconds. Invalidating /dashboard once beats invalidating dozens of individual stock tags. The cache lifetime matters more than granular invalidation here.

Applications with infrequent, targeted mutations favor tags. A content management system might publish one article per day. Invalidating only that article's cache entries preserves every other cached page. Cache hit rates stay high even with daily updates.

Deployment architecture forces the decision in multi-container environments. Teams running on serverless platforms or container orchestrators must implement external cache coordination regardless of primitive choice. At that point, tag-based invalidation provides strictly more power for the same infrastructure cost.

Multi-container deployment diagram showing cache coordination challenges

The primitives combine in mature applications. Core shared data uses tags for surgical invalidation. Peripheral features with isolated data use paths. A product catalog relies on revalidateTag('product:*') while an admin settings panel uses revalidatePath('/admin/settings').

Production applications require explicit cache control beyond Next.js automatic caching. The unstable_cache function provides programmatic cache management with support for both revalidation primitives. Despite its name, the API has remained stable since Next.js 14.0 as covered in Next.js caching patterns.

The third parameter to unstable_cache accepts a tags array. These tags enable surgical invalidation through revalidateTag. The function also accepts a revalidate number setting time-based expiration. Combining both strategies provides defense in depth: tags for immediate invalidation, time-based revalidation as a safety net.

Server Actions coordinate cache invalidation with data mutations. The Next.js revalidation guide documents two timing options: revalidateTag for stale-while-revalidate semantics and updateTag for immediate expiration. Most applications prefer revalidateTag with its 'max' stale window.

The pattern separates concerns effectively. Data fetching functions declare their cache behavior through tags and expiration. Server Actions handle mutations and trigger invalidation. Components simply consume the cached functions without knowing cache semantics exist.

Teams often create cache utilities to standardize tagging conventions and prevent duplicate cache keys:

This abstraction prevents tag typos and ensures consistent cache lifetimes across related functions. The utilities also provide a single place to change cache configuration when requirements evolve.

The key insight appears in production debugging. When a cache entry does not invalidate as expected, developers need to verify three things: the tags in unstable_cache match the tags in revalidateTag, the cache key remains consistent across calls, and the revalidation actually executes in the deployed environment.

The revalidation primitives fail silently in distributed deployments when relying on Next.js default in-memory caching. A user updates a product on container A. The Server Action calls revalidateTag and invalidates the in-memory cache on container A. Container B still serves stale product data because its cache never received the invalidation signal.

This failure mode is subtle because it works perfectly during development. Local development runs a single Next.js process where all invalidations happen in the same memory space. Staging environments often use single containers for cost reasons, hiding the problem until production deploys multiple instances.

The failure compounds with load balancer behavior. Modern load balancers distribute requests across containers for fault tolerance and performance. A user might see fresh data on one request and stale data on the next, depending on which container handles the request. This creates a trust problem where users question whether their updates actually saved.

Diagram showing distributed cache invalidation failure across containers

The solution requires an external cache store that all containers share. Redis provides the standard choice for session stores and distributed caches. The Next.js runtime caching considerations document that serverless environments may not persist cache entries across invocations, requiring external storage for reliability.

Teams running on platforms like Google Cloud Run or AWS Lambda encounter this problem immediately. Each function invocation potentially runs in a fresh container with empty cache. The Payload CMS discussion on cache invalidation shows real production teams discovering this after deployment when users report seeing stale content.

Custom cache adapters bridge Next.js cache APIs to external stores. The adapter intercepts revalidateTag and revalidatePath calls, translating them to cache operations in Redis or another shared store:

This implementation stores cache entries in Redis with standard expiration. Each tag maintains a Redis set containing all cache keys associated with that tag. Invalidating a tag looks up the set, deletes all associated keys, and removes the set itself.

The distributed coordination problem affects both primitives equally. revalidatePath and revalidateTag both require synchronization across containers. Path invalidation might seem simpler because it avoids tagging infrastructure, but the fundamental coordination challenge remains identical.

The correct solution accepts that distributed caching requires shared storage. Using Redis or another external cache eliminates the coordination problem entirely. All containers read and write the same cache store, so invalidation becomes instantaneous across the deployment.

Distributed cache architecture diagram showing Redis coordination

Serverless platforms often provide managed cache services that integrate with application code. Vercel's native edge caching handles this automatically for applications deployed on their platform. Teams deploying elsewhere must implement cache adapters manually or choose managed services that provide Next.js-compatible cache backends.

The infrastructure tradeoff becomes clear: single-container deployments avoid external cache dependencies at the cost of limited scalability. Multi-container deployments require shared cache stores but support horizontal scaling and fault tolerance. The revalidation primitive choice matters less than the cache storage architecture at this scale.

The decision between revalidatePath and revalidateTag depends on data sharing patterns, mutation frequency, and deployment constraints. A systematic framework prevents premature optimization while identifying genuine scaling bottlenecks.

Start by mapping which routes share data. Applications where most data appears on a single route favor path invalidation. A landing page builder might have dedicated data for each page URL. Invalidating /pages/homepage never affects /pages/pricing. The routes share no data, so tags provide no benefit.

Applications where data appears across many routes require tags. E-commerce catalogs display products on listing pages, detail pages, search results, cart views, and recommendation widgets. Invalidating a product means invalidating entries across all these routes. Tracking paths becomes impossible while tagging the product once handles every location.

Decision framework flowchart for choosing revalidation primitive

Mutation patterns influence granularity requirements. Applications with bulk updates might invalidate entire sections. A news aggregator might refresh all articles in a category when the feed updates. Invalidating the category path once beats invalidating hundreds of individual article tags.

Applications with targeted mutations benefit from precise invalidation. A project management tool updates one task at a time. Invalidating only that task's cache entries keeps every other cached task fresh. Cache hit rates stay high even with constant updates.

Deployment architecture often makes the decision. Teams running on managed platforms with built-in distributed caching can use tags freely. The platform handles coordination across containers. Teams running on traditional infrastructure must weigh external cache implementation cost against path invalidation maintainability problems.

The framework suggests starting with path invalidation during early development. Routes typically contain isolated data while teams validate product direction. As applications mature and routes begin sharing data, migrate to tag-based invalidation. This evolution matches natural application growth.

Teams tracking cache hit rates gain concrete data for decisions. If path invalidation maintains hit rates above 80%, tags might be premature. If hit rates drop below 50% despite proper cache lifetimes, path invalidation likely invalidates too broadly. The metrics reveal whether the current approach scales.

The Next.js caching mental model provides context for how these primitives fit into the broader caching system. Revalidation represents only one part of cache strategy. Time-based expiration, stale-while-revalidate semantics, and cache warming also affect overall performance.

Use revalidatePath when routes operate independently with dedicated data, such as admin dashboards where each page manages distinct resources. The primitive also works well during early development before data sharing patterns emerge. Teams should migrate to tags once multiple routes begin displaying the same underlying data.

revalidateTag uses stale-while-revalidate semantics where old content serves while fresh content generates in the background. updateTag immediately expires cache entries, ensuring users see updated data on the next request. Use updateTag only in Server Actions where read-your-own-writes matters, such as after creating a new resource that must appear in a list immediately.

Applications frequently combine both primitives. Core shared entities like products or users use tags for surgical invalidation. Peripheral features with isolated data like settings pages use path invalidation. The combination reduces maintenance burden while preserving cache efficiency where it matters most.

Cache entries remain valid until their time-based expiration triggers. The Next.js revalidation documentation explains that cacheLife profiles set expiration windows from 1 second to 1 year depending on data volatility. Entries expire and regenerate automatically even without explicit invalidation.

Distributed deployments require external cache stores like Redis or managed services that synchronize cache state across containers. Next.js default in-memory cache cannot coordinate across processes, causing silent failures where some containers serve stale data. Teams must implement custom cache adapters or use platforms with built-in distributed caching.

The difference between revalidatePath and revalidateTag determines whether cache invalidation remains manageable as applications grow. Path invalidation works immediately but collapses when routes share data. Tag invalidation requires upfront tagging discipline but scales linearly with application complexity.

Teams should start with concrete metrics. Track cache hit rates, response times, and invalidation frequency. Applications maintaining high hit rates with path invalidation should keep using it until metrics suggest otherwise. Applications with declining cache effectiveness need surgical tag-based invalidation.

The infrastructure decision matters more than the primitive choice at scale. Distributed deployments require external cache coordination regardless of invalidation strategy. Teams should implement shared cache storage early if multi-container deployment is planned. The Next.js 15 caching changes provide context for how the caching system evolved to handle these distributed scenarios.

The correct approach combines both primitives based on data sharing patterns. Tag shared entities for surgical invalidation. Use paths for isolated features. Measure cache performance to validate the strategy. Build external cache infrastructure before scaling beyond single containers.

The multi-container point is the one that bites people. Tags don't help much if each instance keeps its own in-memory cache, so a shared cache handler is basically needed once you scale out.

#9721. 'python' Is Not Recognized as an Internal or External Command: Every Fix

Posted on Nov 20 • Originally published at knowledgemarkg.com

You install Python on Windows, open a terminal, type python and get this:

It almost never means Python failed to install. It means the terminal looked in every folder on your PATH and none of them had a python.exe in it. The fix depends on which of five similar messages you have, so this post starts there.

I reproduced each one on 20 November 2026 on a Windows 11 PC that has Python 3.13 (classic installer) and Python 3.14 (the new Python install manager) side by side. I didn't change any system settings. Instead I ran each command with a cut-down PATH, so every output below is copied from a real terminal. The one exception is the Microsoft Store message, which I couldn't trigger on this PC. That's explained in its section.

The five messages, what each means and the fix.

Before you touch any settings, try the launcher:

With my PATH stripped down to just C:\Windows, python failed but py still worked. On this PC the classic installer's launcher is C:\Windows\py.exe, a folder that is always on PATH, and the install manager provides py as an app alias. If py answers, Python is installed and only PATH is wrong. The second command prints where the real python.exe lives, and that folder is what you'll add. If py is also "not recognized", Python isn't installed. Get it from python.org (next section) rather than searching for a fix.

This is cmd's wording. Python is installed, but its folder isn't on PATH, usually because the "Add python.exe to PATH" box in the installer wasn't ticked. You have two ways out:

Then close the terminal and open a new one. A terminal reads PATH once, when it starts, so the old window keeps saying "not recognized" even after the fix is correct. That catches a lot of people.

The Python docs now recommend the Python install manager from python.org. They say the traditional full installer is "deprecated since 3.14 and will not be produced for Python 3.16 or later". The install manager asks once whether to add %LocalAppData%\Python\bin to PATH. Say yes.

Same cause, PowerShell's wording: CommandNotFoundException means no folder on PATH holds a python.exe. The fixes are the same as above. One PowerShell-only trap: if Python's folder is on PATH and you still get this, check that you aren't typing python3. The classic installer doesn't create a python3.exe. The install manager does, but its docs say it is "not meant to be widely used or recommended". On Windows, use python or py.

This message comes from Windows, not from Python:

Windows ships a python.exe placeholder in %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\WindowsApps, which is on PATH by default. If no real Python comes earlier in PATH, the placeholder runs. With arguments it prints this message, and with none it opens the Store page. I couldn't reproduce it here because on this PC the WindowsApps aliases point at the installed Python install manager, which is how the install manager provides python and py. So the text above is Windows' own message, quoted as users report it.

This one has its own cause. I put C:\Python313 on PATH but left out its Scripts folder, which is a common half-finished manual fix:

pip.exe lives in Scripts, not next to python.exe. You can add Scripts to PATH as well, but there's a better habit: always run pip through Python.

python -m pip works whenever python works, and it can't install into the wrong Python. That second point matters, as the next section shows.

If you have more than one Python, python, py and pip can each point at a different one. On my PC:

python runs 3.13, because C:\Python313 comes first in PATH. py runs 3.14, the install manager's default. And pip is 3.13's. Pillow is installed for 3.13 only, so the same two-line script behaves differently depending on the command:

Nothing is broken. The package was installed for one interpreter and the script ran on the other. The fix is python -m pip (or py -m pip) with the same command you use to run the script, and where python shows you which Python runs first. A virtual environment removes the question entirely:

Inside an activated venv, python and pip both belong to the venv, whatever PATH says.

VS Code's integrated terminal inherits PATH from VS Code, and VS Code read it when it started. If you changed PATH while VS Code was open, close all VS Code windows and start it again. Opening a new terminal tab isn't enough. If it still fails, open a normal cmd window and run where python. If it fails there too, the problem is PATH, not VS Code. For running and debugging, VS Code uses the interpreter you choose with Python: Select Interpreter (Ctrl+Shift+P). Pick the same one you install packages into.

Once Python runs, local AI tools are a common next step. My guide to running DeepSeek R1 locally on Windows, macOS and Linux picks up from there.

Why is python not recognized as an internal or external command?

Windows can't find python.exe in any folder on your PATH. Python is usually installed, but its folder wasn't added, often because the 'Add python.exe to PATH' box was unticked. Try py --version: if it works, either use py or add Python's folder to PATH and open a new terminal.

How do I add Python to PATH on Windows 11?

Run py -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)" to find the folder. Then open Start, search 'environment variables', choose 'Edit environment variables for your account', edit Path, add that folder (and its Scripts folder for pip), and open a new terminal.

What does 'Python was not found; run without arguments to install from the Microsoft Store' mean?

Windows ran its placeholder python.exe from the WindowsApps folder because no real Python came earlier on PATH. Install Python from python.org, or if Python is already installed, move its folder above WindowsApps in Path or turn off the python.exe app execution aliases.

Why is pip not recognized when python works?

pip.exe is in Python's Scripts folder, which is a separate PATH entry. Use python -m pip install requests (or any package name) instead. It always uses the same Python you run, so packages can't end up in a different interpreter.

What is the difference between py and python on Windows?

python runs whichever python.exe comes first on PATH. py is the launcher, which picks an installed version itself (the newest or the configured default) and accepts -3.13 or -V:3.14 to choose. On a PC with two versions they can run different Pythons.

Why do I get No module named after pip install?

pip installed the package into a different Python than the one running your script. Run pip as python -m pip (or py -m pip) using the same command you run the script with, check with where python, or use a virtual environment.

Why is python still not recognized in VS Code after fixing PATH?

VS Code reads PATH when it starts, and its terminals inherit that copy. Close every VS Code window and reopen it. Also select the interpreter with Python: Select Interpreter so running and debugging use the same Python.

#9720. Building MCP Servers for My Own Products: Introducing the Workflow

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I used to manage my products through dashboards. Check analytics here, schedule posts there, pull metrics from another tab. Constant context-switching.

Now, I do all of it by talking to Claude.

Not through some hacked-together integration: through MCP servers I built for my own products. Model Context Protocol is the standard Anthropic published for giving AI assistants structured access to external tools. I built servers for both Spellcast and Lunary. Here's how, and why it changed everything.

MCP is a protocol that lets you define a set of "tools", which are functions with typed inputs and outputs that Claude can call during a conversation. Instead of copy-pasting data into a chat window, Claude calls your API directly and works with the live result.

The architecture: your MCP server exposes tools over stdio (or HTTP). Claude Code discovers them and can call them when relevant. You write the server once; it works in any MCP-compatible client.

Spellcast is my social scheduling platform. The MCP server exposes the full API as typed tools:

What I can do from a Claude conversation:

The practical workflow: I describe what I want, and Claude calls the tools. "Optimize the hooks on my scheduled tweets" becomes Claude reading every post, identifying weak openers, and rewriting them in batches.

Lunary is my astrology platform. The MCP exposes product analytics and content tools:

Me: "Check Lunary metrics and tell me what's changed since last week."

Claude calls get_dashboard, get_dau_wau_mau, get_cohort_retention. Returns a summary. Surfaces what moved.

Me: "Schedule a thread about the SEO growth for the sammii account."

Claude calls list_account_sets to find the right persona, get_brand_voice to load my voice profile, generate_content to write five thread variations, presents them, waits for my pick, then calls create_post to schedule it.

Me: "Those tweets from February with weak hooks, fix them."

Claude calls list_posts for the date range, reads each one, identifies weak openers, writes improvements, calls update_post in batches.

No dashboards. No tab-switching. Just conversation with full product access.

Your product's API is now accessible from any Claude conversation.

The power isn't just convenience. Claude can operate across your entire product context in a single conversation: read your analytics, read your content queue, read your brand voice, and produce work that's coherent across all of them without you manually bridging the gap.

I estimate MCP saves me 5-8 hours a week in dashboard time and manual data-pulling.

More importantly, it removes the friction that stops small tasks from getting done. If checking metrics requires three tabs and a copy-paste, you do it less. If it's one sentence, you do it constantly and catch things early.

#9719. What is piloncillo? This sweetener makes great cookies, pan dulce, and more: Use this traditional Mexican unrefined sugar for a dash of flavor and history.

This article is part of our feature celebrating Pan Dulce. Find all things pan dulce here.

Categorically, piloncillo is a “non-centrifugal” cane sugar, meaning it is an unrefined sugar product and a true natural brown sugar. It’s mostly consumed in Mexico and Latin America, but a similar product can be found in Asia, known as jaggery in India. Though often lumped together, these unrefined dark sugars are very different from brown sugars on the market today, which have been refined to a large degree — in some cases, they’re actually just white sugar with coloring or molasses added.

Making piloncillo, on the other hand, involves an artisanal process that’s hundreds of years old. To make it, pressed cane juice is boiled to evaporate the water and deeply caramelize the sugar. The cooked cane is then poured into molds (often made of wood) and left to dry and harden. Traditional piloncillo is conical in shape and can vary in size from small to large cones but is most commonly found in a medium size that weighs about 200 grams. In Guatemala and Colombia, it is called panela, where it is cooked to a lighter degree and typically formed into a brick, rather than cone, shape. Other forms of piloncillo can be granulated or liquid (which is more rare).

Minimally processed and boldly flavored, piloncillo was historically a prized and respected foodstuff. As an unrefined cane sugar, piloncillo provides more complex vitamins and minerals than refined sugars, which undergo processing and whitening methods that also strip nutrients from the whole food. And piloncillo is also great for baking, providing notes of burnt caramel and hints of smoke. Plus, its rich molasses qualities keep baked goods moist and fresh for longer.

Always look at the ingredient label when purchasing piloncillo and make sure it says 100% pure cane juice or cane sugar. It is becoming increasingly common to find imitation products marketed as jaggery or piloncillo that contain coloring and corn syrup. You can find good piloncillo at specialty grocery stores or online at retailers.

In Mexico and throughout Latin America, piloncillo is an important ingredient in many traditional dishes. (Some will even say it’s not the “real dish” if you substitute sugar in these recipes due to the deep flavors and richness that only piloncillo can provide.) This deep, dark unrefined sugar lends its characteristic flavor and texture to popular foods and beverages such as capirotada, tepache, coyotas, atole, café de olla, calabaza al horno, coricos, and hojarascas, to name a few!

I love adding piloncillo when I’m making champurrado. In this warm and thick chocolate beverage, the piloncillo is chopped or grated and dissolved in the pot with water or milk before adding the chocolate and masa. In this recipe, the piloncillo’s intense sweet and smoky flavors pair well with the chocolate and corn masa.

While there are many dishes and uses for piloncillo, it’s not a simple substitution for granulated white sugar in recipes, but you can use it the same as you would brown sugar with a 1:1 substitution by weight.  Depending on how hard the cone is, it can be crumbled or grated for easier measuring. If it is very hard, try cutting it in half with a sharp knife and then placing it between parchment paper or a towel and beating with a rolling pin.

#9717. How a Claude Code session froze my Mac with a 288 GB text file

My Mac suddenly became unresponsive this morning. The disk was almost full, and one text file in /tmp had grown to 288 GB in about 12 minutes.

I run a lot of Claude Code sessions at once, so the first question was which one, if any, was writing it.

lsof lists the processes that have a file open:

It showed a cat and a grep. Walking up the parent chain with ps -o pid,ppid,command -p led from both of them to shells started by the same Claude Code session.

That session was running a design review over a set of pages. Each review wrote a small text file of findings, and the last step combined them into one file:

The output file is review-all.txt, and that name also matches review-*.txt.

The redirect at the end applies to the whole loop, so the shell creates review-all.txt before it expands the glob. The new, empty output file lands in the list of inputs. When the loop reaches it, cat starts reading the file it is appending to. Every block it reads is written back onto the end, so the end of the file moves away as fast as cat reads, and cat never gets there.

The one-line version has the same trap, with a delay:

Here the glob is expanded before the redirect creates the file, so the first run is fine. On the second run the old review-all.txt is one of the inputs, and the loop starts. Agents rerun commands all the time.

I ran the same loop on a Linux machine with GNU coreutils and got this:

GNU cat checks whether an input is the same file as its output and skips it. The cat that ships with macOS comes from BSD and has no such check, so it keeps going until a write fails. Mine stopped on its own after 12 minutes, probably when a write failed for lack of space. By then the file held 288 GB, about 400 MB for every second it ran, and the disk was 96% full.

The command ran into the agent's 10-minute command timeout, so the tool moved it to the background and the agent went on with other work. Two more full reads of the file followed:

Both were still running when I found the file. Neither changed it, but together they kept the disk busy reading hundreds of gigabytes. A person in a hurry could have written every one of these commands.

Stop anything that still has the file open before you delete it. Deleting a file only removes its name; the space comes back when the last process holding it closes.

Free space went from 37 GiB back to 306 GiB.
