#9707. Xcode Instruments in Practice: Profiling and Optimizing iOS Apps

Most performance bugs I've chased in production iOS apps didn't come from code that was obviously slow. They came from code that was fine with test data and fell over with real data. Think of a list that scrolls smoothly with 20 items and stutters with 2,000, or a screen that opens instantly on a new iPhone and takes a second on a three-year-old one. A sort that runs on the main thread "because it's fast", until someone's account has eight years of history.

You can't find these by reading code. You find them by measuring. Xcode Instruments is the tool Apple gives us for that. This article walks through the workflow I use: profile, investigate, optimize, verify. It uses real Swift 6 code and the Instruments features in current Xcode releases.

Instruments is a profiling tool that comes with Xcode. It records various aspects of your app and the system over time, including CPU samples, allocations, thread states, signposts, and SwiftUI updates. These metrics are displayed as tracks on a shared timeline, allowing you to correlate events like a CPU spike with specific user interactions or system hangs.

You can access Instruments through Product → Profile (⌘I), which builds your app with the scheme's Profile action and launches Instruments attached to it. Alternatively, you can open Instruments from Xcode → Open Developer Tool → Instruments and attach it to a running process.

The debugger provides insights into what is happening at a specific line of code, whereas Instruments helps you understand where time and memory are spent across a complete workflow. Breakpoints can disrupt timing, making them unsuitable for profiling. The debug navigator's CPU and memory gauges indicate that something is expensive but don't specify what. Instruments uses sampling and low-overhead tracing, ensuring your app runs close to real speed while recording.

By default, the Profile action uses the Release configuration, which is crucial for accurate profiling. Debug builds compile Swift without optimization (-Onone), so generics aren't specialized, nothing is inlined, and retain/release traffic is much higher. A function that dominates a Debug profile may not appear in a Release build, and the actual bottleneck might not be visible. Always profile using the same configuration you ship, and if you need additional logging or symbols, add them to a Release-based configuration.

The Simulator runs on your Mac's CPU, memory, GPU, and storage, not on iPhone hardware. Timing data from the Simulator doesn't accurately reflect an iPhone's behavior. Use the Simulator for logic-level checks, such as verifying function calls or detecting leaks. For real profiling, use a physical device, preferably an older model at the lower end of your supported range. This setup provides more accurate insights into thermal state, memory pressure, and GPU behavior.

When you start a recording, Instruments asks for a template, which is a preconfigured set of instruments. Picking the right one saves a lot of guesswork.

Time Profiler is the usual starting point. The rest of this article explains when it isn't enough.

Time Profiler samples the call stack of every thread at a fixed interval, typically every millisecond. Functions appearing frequently in samples have consumed significant CPU time. It doesn't trace every call, keeping overhead low enough to profile real workflows.

Take a hypothetical example: a loadFeed() function shows a Total Weight of 900 ms and a Self Weight of 2 ms. loadFeed() itself is cheap, but its callees are expensive. Expand loadFeed() and keep following the heavy branch. Inside, you find decodePosts() (Total 850 ms, Self 15 ms) and under that DateFormatter.date(from:) with a high Self Weight. That's where the CPU burned: you're creating or using a date formatter for every post.

High total with low self means keep drilling down. High self means this function's own work is the cost. In an inverted call tree, the top entries sorted by Self Weight are your hotspots.

Since Instruments 16 (Xcode 16), call-tree data can also be shown as a Flame Graph. Switch the detail view between Call Tree, Flame Graph and Top Functions from the jump bar above the detail area. Apple introduced it in What's new in Xcode 16.

You're looking for wide plateaus: a wide box with nothing (or very little) on top of it. Those are functions burning CPU in their own code, the visual equivalent of high Self Weight. A tall, narrow spike is a deep call stack that's cheap overall, so you can usually ignore it.

Top Functions flattens the call tree into a list of functions by weight, regardless of where they were called from. This catches a pattern the call tree hides: a small helper called from fifty places. In the call tree its cost is spread across fifty branches and each looks harmless. In Top Functions, it's one row near the top.

Here's a search screen that filters contacts on every keystroke:

In the flame graph, the widest plateau sits on String.folding(options:locale:), under matches(_:query:), under the view's filtering code. Top Functions shows folding and the string allocations from + as the top entries. The query is re-normalized once per contact instead of once per keystroke, and every contact's name is re-normalized on every keystroke.

The fix is to normalize each contact once, when contacts load, and the query once per keystroke:

Not every wide box is worth fixing. I rank candidates by three things:

Time Profiler tells you where CPU goes, but it doesn't pinpoint the duration of specific operations like "open the invoice screen" or distinguish between network wait and decoding times. For that, you need to mark the operation yourself using signposts. OSSignposter (iOS 15+) is the Swift API in the OSLog framework.

Profile with Time Profiler. Your intervals appear in the Points of Interest track (or in an os_signpost track if you add the instrument). Then:

This is also the key to fair before-and-after comparisons, covered later.

The six examples below are realistic but hypothetical. They're patterns I've seen in real apps, simplified for the article. Any timings mentioned are illustrative, not measurements.

The issue. A sales report screen groups and totals thousands of orders. The grouping runs in body, which runs on the main actor, so the screen freezes when it opens and again every time the date range changes.

Why it's inefficient. SwiftUI can evaluate body many times, and each evaluation repeats the full grouping on the main thread. With enough orders, one evaluation is longer than a frame, so you get hitches. Past a few hundred milliseconds, it's a hang.

The fix. Compute the rows once per input change, off the main actor, and keep the UI update on the main actor:

Only the computation moves off the main actor. The view and its @State stay on the main actor, where SwiftUI expects them. Don't move UI updates off the main actor to "speed them up": UIKit and SwiftUI aren't thread-safe, and Swift 6 will (rightly) refuse to compile most attempts.

Verify. Add a signpost interval around the computation and profile with Time Profiler, filtered to the main thread. The grouping should disappear from the main thread and appear on a cooperative-pool thread. In the Hangs track, opening the screen should no longer produce a hang.

The issue. A photo grid decodes each full-resolution image to show a 100-point thumbnail.

Why it's inefficient. UIImage(data:) doesn't decode immediately: decoding happens lazily when the image is first rendered, on the main thread. A 12-megapixel photo decodes to about 48 MB (4 bytes per pixel), and you only display about 300×300 pixels of it. Time Profiler shows image-decoding frames under the render pass. Allocations shows large, short-lived image buffers. Apple covers this in Image and Graphics Best Practices (WWDC18).

The fix. Downsample with ImageIO so only a thumbnail-sized bitmap is ever decoded, and do it off the main actor:

kCGImageSourceShouldCacheImmediately matters here: without it, the actual decode can still be deferred to render time on the main thread, which undoes the work of moving it off.

Verify. In Time Profiler, image decoding frames should leave the main thread. In Allocations, filter by VM: ImageIO / CG raster data while scrolling. Expect far smaller buffers and a much lower peak. Animation Hitches should show fewer late frames while scrolling.

The issue. An inbox shows "5 min ago" labels. To keep them fresh, the store publishes the current time every second.

Why it's inefficient. With ObservableObject, any @Published change sends objectWillChange. Every view observing the store, here the whole inbox, re-evaluates its body every second. Every visible row re-evaluates too, because its now input changed. That's a lot of work to change one label.

The fix. Two changes. Let Text render relative dates itself, so no clock state is needed. And use the Observation framework (@Observable, iOS 17+), which tracks which properties each body reads:

Self._printChanges() inside a body is a quick debugging aid that logs what triggered an update. It's underscored and unofficial, so use it only while debugging and remove it before shipping.

Verify. Profile with the SwiftUI template. Before the change, the view body updates track shows InboxView and every visible MessageRow updating once per second while nothing is happening. After it, idle periods should show essentially no body updates. In Xcode 26 and later, the Cause & Effect Graph shows which state change triggered an update. If a view updates more often than you expect, that graph tells you why.

The issue. A transactions list creates formatters inside each row's body.

Why it's inefficient. DateFormatter and NumberFormatter are expensive to create: they load locale and calendar data. Creating two per row per body evaluation, while scrolling, means thousands of short-lived formatters. Time Profiler shows the cost in formatter setup. Allocations shows a large count of transient NSDateFormatter and NSNumberFormatter objects.

The fix. Create the formatter once and reuse it. Views are @MainActor, so a static property on the view is isolated to the main actor too. That keeps a non-Sendable formatter safe under Swift 6 strict concurrency:

The currency side uses FormatStyle (.currency(code:)), which avoids managing a formatter object yourself. Don't assume it's free, though: measure it the same way.

Verify. In Allocations, record a scroll through the list and search for DateFormatter. Before the change, the Transient count climbs with every row. After it, there should be one persistent instance. The Generations feature (Mark Generation before and after the scroll) shows what was allocated during just that workflow.

The issue. A feed shows avatars. Ten rows by the same author appear at once, and each starts its own download of the same URL.

Why it's inefficient. This looks safe, because it's an actor, but actors are reentrant. While the first caller is suspended at await URLSession..., the actor accepts the next call. That call also finds the cache empty and starts a second download. The cache only helps after the first download finishes.

The fix. Cache the in-flight task, not just the result, so concurrent callers share one download:

The entry is stored before the first await. That's what makes it work: any call that arrives during the download sees .loading and joins it.

Verify. Profile with the Network instrument (or check your server logs). Ten rows by one author should produce one request, not ten. With Swift Concurrency, you'll also see far fewer download tasks.

The issue. A thumbnail store does CPU-heavy rendering inside the actor.

Why it's inefficient. An actor runs one piece of isolated code at a time. ThumbnailRenderer.render is synchronous and runs while the actor is held, so twenty thumbnails render one after another even on a six-core phone. Every other call, including instant cache hits, waits behind the current render. In the Swift Concurrency instrument, this shows up as a long queue of tasks waiting on ThumbnailStore. In Time Profiler, only one thread is busy rendering.

The fix. Keep the actor for what it's good at, protecting the cache, and do the heavy work outside it:

The re-check after the await matters. Any await inside an actor is a point where other calls can run and change its state. Re-validate assumptions after every suspension. Combine this with the in-flight pattern from E if duplicate downloads also matter.

Verify. In the Swift Concurrency instrument, the actor's queue should stay short. In Time Profiler (Separate by Thread), rendering should spread across several threads. Wrap a batch of thumbnails in a signpost interval and compare its duration before and after. On the same device and with the same images, the interval should shrink.

Swift concurrency changes what a bottleneck looks like. These are the concepts that matter most when reading a profile.

The main actor is one serial executor. Every await MainActor.run, every @MainActor method call from a background task, and every UI update queues on it. Each hop is cheap, but thousands of them compete with rendering and touch handling.

(Record and process(_:) stand for your own model type and work function.)

Actors serialize execution, not operations. An actor method that awaits can be interleaved with other calls at each await, as in example E. Performance-wise, two rules follow:

Task { } creates an unstructured task. It inherits the current actor and priority, isn't cancelled with its parent, and nothing waits for it. Creating one per item for a large collection gives you thousands of tasks competing for the cooperative thread pool, which has about one thread per CPU core. That means memory overhead, and work finishing in an unpredictable order.

For "do this for every item," use a task group with bounded concurrency:

Structured child tasks are cancelled with their parent, their results are collected in one place, and the limit keeps memory predictable. Each in-flight render holds a decoded bitmap.

@concurrent functions, Task.detached and the cooperative pool are for CPU work that finishes. Long-running or blocking work, like large synchronous file I/O or a C library that blocks, doesn't belong on the cooperative pool, because it holds a thread that other tasks need. For blocking work, use a dedicated DispatchQueue or Thread and bridge back with a continuation.

This is the most important distinction for reading profiles:

Don't count on the compiler to catch this. Swift 6 happens to reject this exact snippet because the task mutates a captured var, but wrap the result in a lock-protected box and it compiles cleanly: blocking itself is never a compile error. In a trace, it shows up as a thread in a blocked state in System Trace, and in Time Profiler as a thread that's alive but has almost no samples.

The WWDC sessions Swift concurrency: Behind the scenes and Visualize and optimize Swift concurrency go deeper on the thread pool and the Swift Concurrency instrument.

An optimization isn't done until you've measured it on the same workflow, on the same device, under the same conditions.

Instruments keeps multiple runs in one trace document: record again, and the new run appears next to the old one. Since Xcode 26.4, you can compare call trees between runs directly. Use View → Detail Area → Compare With… or the ⇆ button in the jump bar. Functions that got slower are marked as regressions and functions that got faster as improvements. You can also bring recordings into one document with File → Import As Run…. See the Xcode 26.4 release notes and Profile, fix, and verify: Improve app responsiveness with Instruments (WWDC26).

The numbers below are illustrative only, made up to show how to lay out a comparison, not measurements from a real app.

Time Profiler only sees threads that are running. Many performance issues occur when threads are not running:

If the UI is frozen but the CPU track is nearly flat, the main thread isn't doing expensive work; it's waiting. Common causes include:

Time Profiler shows little activity because there's little to sample. System Trace reveals the main thread in a blocked state and what it's waiting on. Apple describes this "blocked main thread" pattern in Analyze hangs with Instruments (WWDC23).

Before a release, I run through this list:

The workflow is the same regardless of the symptom:

Most fixes in this article are small. The challenge lies in identifying which small change matters, and Instruments is the tool that provides that insight.

Optimizing without measuring can lead to mistakes in both directions. You might spend a day speeding up code that wasn't the issue, or release a "faster" version that merely shifts the cost elsewhere. A recording, however, costs just a few minutes and definitively answers the question.

What is Xcode Instruments used for? Instruments is Apple's profiling app, included with Xcode. It records CPU usage, memory allocations, leaks, hangs, SwiftUI updates, Swift concurrency activity, and more on a shared timeline, helping you identify what makes an app slow or memory-hungry.

Should I profile in the Simulator or on a device? For timing-related profiling, use a physical device. The Simulator runs on your Mac's hardware, so its timings don't reflect iPhone performance accurately. It's still useful for logic checks, such as call counts or memory leaks.

What's the difference between Self Weight and Total Weight in Time Profiler? Total Weight includes the time spent in the functions a function calls. Self Weight counts only the function's own code. If the Total Weight is high but the Self Weight is low, the cost is likely deeper in the call tree. If the Self Weight is high, the function itself is expensive.

How do I measure one specific operation in Instruments? Wrap the operation in an OSSignposter interval (beginInterval / endInterval), using a signposter with the .pointsOfInterest category. The interval will appear in the Points of Interest track, and you can set it as the inspection range to filter other instruments to that operation.

Why does my app freeze when Time Profiler shows low CPU? The main thread might be blocked, not busy, due to waiting on a lock, a semaphore, synchronous I/O, or another thread. Use the Hangs instrument to find the freeze, and System Trace to see what the main thread was waiting for.

#9705. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

#9704. Seven Spheres Became an App: Here's How

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

I’m a full-stack engineer specialising in front-end development & design engineering

There is a photograph I took in 2017, on the floor of a university library, of an open copy of Jonathan Black's The Secret History of the World. The page is the one where Black describes the planetary sequence: Saturn, the Sun, Venus, the Moon, and Jupiter, weaving the conditions that made life on Earth possible. I remember taking it because I wanted to remember the exact page. I did not think anything further about what I would do with it.

Nine years later, I opened my laptop this morning to an analytics dashboard for a piece of software I have been building for two years. Forty-three thousand people visited the site last month. Most of them came in through articles in the grimoire, a knowledge base I have built out to roughly two thousand entries on planetary correspondences, crystals, herbs, spells, runes, tarot, and the relationships between them.

The library, and the dashboard. Twenty-one and twenty-nine. Six years apart. I have only recently been able to say, out loud, that these are the same project.

Most MA research ends at graduation. You hand in the thesis, the external examiners sign off, the degree is conferred, and the research becomes a document you put in a drawer. That is not a failure mode; that is what most research is for. It proves you can do the work, and then you stop.

Mine did not stop, because the research had planted a question I could not answer with more reading. It was something like: if the Hermetic cosmology is internally coherent across two thousand years of texts, across Egyptian and Greek and Latin and Coptic translation, across Black and Mead and Everard and Freke and Gandy, and if it describes a specific mechanism by which consciousness enters a body through seven planetary spheres, then what would that mechanism look like rendered in software?

I did not have a coherent answer at 23. I did not even know I was asking the question. I knew I had painted invisible sentences onto the inside walls of a cube. I knew I thought the Wordsworth line was the most important sentence I had ever read. I knew something in the Corpus Hermeticum had landed with me and would not leave.

When I started building Lunary in May 2024, I was not thinking about the MA. I was thinking about a technical problem: existing astrology platforms were either dated, credulous, or marketed as entertainment, and I believed there was room for something that took the underlying system seriously. It was only about six months in, writing the knowledge schema for the grimoire, that I realised I was building the thesis I had written at 22. In code this time, and in Postgres tables, and in the way the birth chart calculator consumed a VSOP87 ephemeris and turned it into a set of quality assignments.

Here is what Lunary is, if you read it through the Hermetic frame I spent nine months in the library building.

The birth chart is the record of the qualities your consciousness acquired as it descended through the seven spheres. That is the reading Parts 4 and 5 of this series made explicit: the soul descends through Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon, picking up a signature quality from each sphere, and the configuration at birth is the local snapshot of that descent. The chart is not a prediction. It is a receipt. Lunary's chart module calculates the positions using astronomy-engine, an open-source VSOP87 implementation in JavaScript, under an MIT licence. No subscription is needed to see the chart. It is the most honest object in the product.

The transit engine is the ongoing conversation between your acquired qualities and the spheres that gave them to you. When Mars moves across the position where the Moon sat at your birth, something that the ancient cosmology would call a conversation is happening between the sphere that contributed your instinct and reflex and the sphere that contributed your capacity for assertion. Whether or not you think that conversation is causal, the conversation is real in the sense that the mapping is real and the geometry is real and the tradition that assigned meaning to the geometry is two thousand years old and internally consistent. Lunary calculates all of this in real time. Thirty-six aspect types across every classical and modern body. The software does the arithmetic. The user does the reading.

The grimoire is the knowledge base. Two thousand articles, encoding the correspondences that have been maintained across cultures and centuries: which herb pairs with which planet, which crystal supports which intention, which tarot card corresponds to which path on the Tree of Life, which rune draws from which branch of Norse cosmology. The correspondences are not my invention. They are the things the tradition has kept stable for long enough that they became the tradition. All I have done is structure them so that a piece of software can retrieve them coherently. The grimoire is the MA bibliography, rewritten as a queryable graph.

The astral guide is the AI layer. I want to be precise about this, because it is the part most likely to be read uncharitably. The astral guide does not fabricate answers. It retrieves passages from the grimoire and the user's own chart context, and it stitches them into a reply. There is no generative astrology. There is no freewheeling fortune-telling.

The model is constrained to surfacing what is already in the knowledge graph. You could, if you wanted, reach the same reply by clicking through ten articles yourself. The AI is there to save the clicks, not to invent the content.

Read in sequence, the four components are a single thing. The chart is the starting state. The transits are the live feed. The grimoire is the library. The astral guide is the librarian. The whole product is a UV light. It shows the reader what was already true about the sky at the moment they were born, and what is already true about the sky right now. The data was always there. The product is the decision about when the UV light comes up.

That sentence is the entire connection between the MA and Lunary. The MA was a cube with invisible quotes; you walked in and could not see them; the UV came on; the sentences appeared. Lunary is a dashboard with invisible relationships; you open it and cannot see them; the calculation runs; the relationships appear. Both are about making something visible that was already present.

I did not plan this. I am telling you, as honestly as I can, that I did not plan this, and that I realised it about eighteen months into building. The thesis had already written the product specification. I just took six years to read back through my own work and notice.

Astrology, as a cultural artefact, has two very different lives.

One is the horoscope column, the thing at the back of the magazine, the daily predictions on the apps that optimise for engagement. That life is loose, entertaining, and often dishonest. It makes claims it cannot justify. It markets certainty it does not have. It is the reason a lot of thoughtful people dismiss astrology before they ever encounter the source material. I do not defend this life. I understand why it is dismissed.

The other life is the cosmology the MA was engaging with. Older, more serious, harder to hold. It is the claim that the ancient world developed a specific framework for thinking about how consciousness enters a body, that the framework uses the planetary sequence as its organising principle, and that the natal chart is the application of this framework to a specific moment in time.

This life does not claim that Venus causes you to like beautiful things. It claims that the sphere conventionally called Venus is associated with the quality conventionally called desire, and that your birth moment is a meaningful location within that framework.

Those are different projects. I am being honest about this because the distinction matters.

Lunary is built for the second project. The grimoire reads more like a philosophical reference than like a lifestyle app. The transit articles walk through the astronomy first and the interpretation second. The astral guide refuses to predict. The industry, largely, markets the first project. I can only build what I think is defensible and see whether it finds an audience.

The claim underneath everything I have ever built is straightforward, and it is the same claim the UV cube made: information that already exists in the world becomes visible when you structure it correctly and put the viewer inside the right affordance. The viewer does not need new information. The world does not need new events. The work is the architecture.

In the cube, that architecture was physical. Fabric panels, UV paint, a specific transition from darkness into invisible light. You walked in, and the sentences appeared. In Lunary, the architecture is software. Schemas, an ephemeris, a knowledge graph, a retrieval layer. You open the app, and the relationships appear. In both cases, the content was already there.

A product is an affordance for perception. A thesis is the same thing in prose. The MA was the argument in an academic register. Lunary is the argument in a commercial one. The argument has not changed; the medium and the reach have.

I want to say this plainly, because the piece does not work without it.

They were started six years apart. They were submitted to completely different audiences. One lives in a university archive and in a stack of printed volumes on my parents' bookshelf. The other lives at a domain name and gets recalculated every minute. But the question underneath them is the same question, and the architecture underneath them is the same architecture, and the claim they are making is the same claim.

At 21, the claim had to be an installation, because I was an MA student with a timber frame and a bolt of fabric and a case of UV paint and a small grant. At 29, the claim has to be a product, because I am a founder with a codebase and a Stripe account and a team of one and a monthly server bill. The medium adapts to what is available. The argument does not.

If the MA taught me anything, it was that ideas survive their original container. The Corpus Hermeticum survived the collapse of the Alexandrian schools, the loss of the library, the burning of the Serapeum, the retranslation through Latin, the Renaissance rediscovery, the Victorian theosophists, the twentieth-century academic sceptics. The ideas did not need the original container. They needed readers who would build the next one.

Lunary is the next container I have been able to build. It is a sincere one. It is the one I know how to make. When I am dead, somebody else will build the container after it, and the ideas will keep going, because the ideas have kept going for two thousand years already and have not run out of structural integrity.

That is the whole series. That is what A Journey Through Light has been arguing, from the first piece to this one. The question is old. The answers are older. The work is making them visible again, in whatever medium the current century hands you to work with.

Thank you for reading this far. The fact that you did is, in its own small way, part of why the project continues.

This is part 7 of A Journey Through Light.

#9696. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#9683. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

#9672. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!
